subChunks.title: Conditionals: if/else & switch-expressions
subChunks.hookHtml: A spell that always fires the same way is a toy. Real magic responds to the situation — to the enemy's weakness, the weather, the phase of the moon. In Java, your code makes decisions using conditionals.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
if / else if / else

int mana = 75;

if (mana >= 100) {
    System.out.println("Full power spell");
} else if (mana >= 50) {
    System.out.println("Half-power spell");
} else {
    System.out.println("No mana — rest!");
}

Conditions use comparison operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) and logical operators (&&, ||, !).

Ternary Operator

A concise one-liner for simple if/else:

String result = (mana >= 50) ? "Cast" : "Rest";
System.out.println(result);

switch-expression (Java 14+)

Modern Java replaces the old fall-through switch statement with the cleaner switch-expression:

String grade = "B";
String feedback = switch (grade) {
    case "A" -> "Outstanding!";
    case "B" -> "Well done.";
    case "C" -> "Acceptable.";
    default  -> "Keep studying.";
};
System.out.println(feedback);

Arrow syntax (->) prevents fall-through automatically and makes the expression return a value directly. You can also use yield for multi-statement cases:

int points = switch (grade) {
    case "A" -> 100;
    case "B" -> {
        System.out.println("Computing B points...");
        yield 80;
    }
    default -> 0;
};

String equality

Never compare strings with == — it checks reference identity, not content. Use .equals():

String spell = "Fireball";
if (spell.equals("Fireball")) { // correct
    System.out.println("Casting!");
}

storyBeats.text: Eldrin leads you into the Academy's training arena. Six different enemies stand at different distances, each with a different weakness.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A spell that fires the same way every time is useless in battle. You must adapt. In Java, this is done with if, else if, and else. The code chooses a branch based on a condition.

storyBeats.speaker: Choosing a spell by mana
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: For quick yes/no choices, the ternary operator is your friend — three operands in one line. Condition, question mark, then the two outcomes separated by a colon.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And when you're matching one value against many cases — a spell school, a direction, a day of the week — use the switch-expression. Modern Java's arrow syntax is clean and prevents the dreaded fall-through bug.

storyBeats.speaker: switch-expression
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: One final warning: comparing Strings with == is a common trap. It checks whether two variables point to the same object, not whether they contain the same text. Always use .equals() for Strings.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Without any starter code, write a health-status reporter for a hero:

  • Set int health = 35.
  • Use if / else if / else to print "Healthy" (health >= 75), "Injured" (health >= 30), or "Critical" (below 30).
  • Use a ternary to set a boolean called needsPotion to true if health < 50, otherwise false. Print it.
  • Use a switch-expression on a String spellSchool = "Frost" to assign a damage bonus: "Fire" → 50, "Frost" → 35, "Lightning" → 45, default → 20. Print the bonus.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between an if/else chain and a switch-expression in Java. When would you choose one over the other? Include a note about why == fails with Strings.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
A different warrior needs assessing. From memory, write the health-status reporter with new values:

  • Set int health = 80.
  • Use if / else if / else to print "Healthy" (health >= 75), "Injured" (health >= 30), or "Critical" (below 30).
  • Use a ternary to set a boolean called needsPotion to true if health < 50, otherwise false. Print it.
  • Use a switch-expression on a String spellSchool = "Lightning" to assign a damage bonus: "Fire" → 50, "Frost" → 35, "Lightning" → 45, default → 20. Print the bonus.

questions.prompt: Which operator is used for logical AND in Java?
questions.explanation: && is the logical AND operator. & is the bitwise AND operator — it evaluates both operands even if the first is false. && short-circuits (stops early if the first operand is false), which is both safer and more efficient.
5 % 2 == 1, not 0, so the condition is false. The ternary returns "odd".

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this String comparison?
questions.answer: Should use s.equals("hello") instead of ==. The == operator compares references, not content.
questions.explanation: == on objects checks whether both variables point to the same memory location. String literals may or may not be the same object depending on whether Java interns them. Always use .equals() for content comparison.

questions.prompt: What advantage does the switch-expression arrow syntax (->) have over the old switch statement with : and break?
options: It prevents fall-through and can return a value directly
It requires fewer lines of code
questions.answer: It prevents fall-through and can return a value directly
questions.explanation: Old switch statements used break to stop fall-through; forgetting it caused all subsequent cases to run. Arrow syntax (->) eliminates fall-through entirely and lets the switch produce a value, making the code cleaner and less error-prone.

subChunks.title: Loops: for, while, and break/continue
subChunks.hookHtml: A wizard who casts a hundred fireballs must not write a hundred lines of code. Loops are the art of repetition — doing the same thing many times, or until a condition is met.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
for loop — when you know how many times

// init; condition; update
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    System.out.println("Round " + i);
}

enhanced for-each — iterating a collection

int[] scores = {85, 90, 72, 95};
for (int s : scores) {
    System.out.println(s);
}

while loop — when the count is unknown

int mana = 100;
while (mana > 0) {
    System.out.println("Casting... mana: " + mana);
    mana -= 20;
}

do-while — runs at least once

int attempts = 0;
do {
    System.out.println("Attempt " + ++attempts);
} while (attempts < 3);

break and continue

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    if (i == 3) continue; // skip 3
    if (i == 7) break;    // stop at 7
    System.out.println(i);
}
// prints: 0 1 2 4 5 6

break exits the loop entirely. continue skips to the next iteration.

Common pitfall: infinite loops

// DANGER: condition never becomes false
while (true) {
    System.out.println("Forever...");
    // forgot to update the condition!
}

Always ensure your loop condition will eventually become false, or use break to exit.

storyBeats.text: Eldrin leads you to a practice dummy that regenerates itself. Fifty identical fireballs are needed to defeat it.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: If I asked you to write System.out.println("Fireball!"); fifty times, you would quit by the third line. Loops are the answer. The for loop has three parts: initialise, check, update.

storyBeats.speaker: for loop
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: When you do not know how many times to loop — perhaps you cast until your mana runs out — use a while loop. The condition is checked before each iteration.

storyBeats.speaker: while loop
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: There is a third loop you must know: do-while. Unlike while, it executes the body first, then checks the condition. The body always runs at least once — useful when you must attempt an action before deciding whether to repeat.

storyBeats.speaker: do-while loop
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Two powerful tools inside any loop: break shatters the loop immediately. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next. Use them sparingly — too many breaks and continues make loops hard to reason about.

storyBeats.speaker: break and continue

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Use a for loop to print the sum of all integers from 1 to 100 inclusive. Print only the final sum (not each number).

Then use a while loop to count down from 10 to 1, printing each number, but skip 5 using continue.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Java's three main loop types — for, while, and do-while — and describe a situation where you'd choose each one. Include an explanation of break and continue.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:

Then use a while loop to count down from 10 to 1, printing each number, but skip 5 using continue.

questions.prompt: How many times does this loop print?
questions.explanation: The loop runs for i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — five values total. The condition i < 5 becomes false when i reaches 5.
continue skips the remaining code in the current iteration and jumps to the loop's update expression (for a for loop) or re-checks the condition (for a while loop).
The do-while always executes at least once. Iterations: x=3, x=6, x=9, x=12. When x=12, the condition 12 < 10 is false, so the loop ends. Final value: 12.

questions.prompt: This loop is supposed to print 1 through 5 but it runs forever. Why?
questions.answer: The loop variable i is never incremented, so i <= 5 is always true — infinite loop. Add i++ inside the loop body.
questions.explanation: A while loop relies on the programmer to update the condition variable. Forgetting i++ means the condition never becomes false, causing an infinite loop.
